title: TSMC’s 2-Nanometer Outpaces 3-Nanometer Growth
author: Daniel Nenni
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

TSMC is preparing another major increase in leading-edge chip production, underscoring the strength of demand for the technologies powering artificial intelligence, smartphones and high-performance computing. According to supply-chain sources, monthly 2-nanometer capacity is targeted to rise from 90,000 wafers at the end of 2026 to 110,000 by mid-2027, a 22% increase. Three-nanometer capacity is expected to grow from more than 180,000 wafers to 210,000 over the same period, an increase exceeding 16%.

The expansion would extend the rapid scaling of TSMC’s 3-nanometer platform, whose monthly capacity reportedly stood at 120,000 to 130,000 wafers at the end of 2025. Although 2-nanometer technology has now become the company’s most advanced production node, sustained customer demand means 3-nanometer manufacturing remains commercially important.

TSMC has not confirmed the reported targets, saying capacity information should come from official company announcements. Nevertheless, the plans are consistent with its enormous investment program. The chipmaker expects 2026 capital expenditure of $60 billion to $64 billion, with roughly 70% to 80% directed toward advanced processes. It is adding 3-nanometer facilities in Taiwan, Arizona and Japan while converting some Taiwanese 5-nanometer equipment.

Why it matters: TSMC manufactures the world’s most sophisticated chips for many leading technology companies, making its capacity decisions a key indicator of future industry demand. Expanding both nodes suggests customers expect AI infrastructure spending and demand for premium processors to remain strong.

More capacity could ease supply constraints, support faster product launches and lift TSMC’s revenue to another record. It also raises execution risks: new fabs and advanced lithography require immense spending, high yields and dependable equipment supply. Success would strengthen TSMC’s technological lead, pricing power and strategic importance, while reinforcing Taiwan’s central role in the global semiconductor ecosystem. It would also signal confidence that leading-edge chip demand can justify historic investment levels for years to come.
